items.title: Allen Toussaint Interview, 1979-03-13
items.q: None of the Lee Dorsey songs would have been written if it wasn't for Lee.

ctx.x: I don't think I've heard any tracks from that. Great. Great if you haven't. Something best left forgotten. Got some tape left on that. In 1965, if I'm not mistaken, we got together with Marshall Seahorn for Sansu Enterprises. And that's when you put out some great things about Lee Dorsey working in the coal mine. Holy Cow. Did those just come to you like driving in the car and things like that? Those are such, I think those kind of define the New Orleans fun song. Things that you always want to sing over and over…

Lee Dorsey's way of being and his voice has a lot to do with those songs being in existence. None of the Lee Dorsey songs would have been written if it wasn't for Lee. I would say that. Well, in a way the same for Irma Thomas, but there are some songs that I wrote for Irma that sound quite normal to me as a normal song. But Lee Dorsey's songs were written where I wouldn't dare draw them on someone else.

Just as you have to have somebody who's fun to work with for songs like Holy Cow and working on a coal mine, do you think that for someone like Irma Thomas and for blues, to get that really real sound that somebody has to have had a certain amount of real pain in their life and be singing that out? Because you don't hear that in a lot of California white musicians today. It's just that they kind of hit rhythm and blues, but they miss something. I don't know if I have all of that question. Okay.
